requirement: Habeas's bundled agent skills and any output that requests or reports a function attestation MUST explain its purpose: after reviewing the function and applicable requirement and example texts, the agent is confirming that the function carries citations for every applicable requirement or named example. The agent MUST explain how it identified the relevant definitions, why its requirements inputs cover them, and how the cited texts account for the function's behavior, including interactions between requirements. Matching input snapshots and a matching citation list alone MUST NOT justify a true determination. A changed function or reviewed definition set MUST be reassessed before its determination is true.
rationale:
All three bundled skills and add-input output explain that attestations confirm all applicable citations after review of a function and relevant requirement and example texts. They direct agents to explain definition discovery, coverage by requirements inputs, and combined behavior, then reassess after changes.

Reviewed the refreshed documentation and skill references. Their current locations and source text are captured; the implemented behavior described by this requirement is unchanged by the authoring and outcome-guidance edits.

text: name: habeas-bootstrap-requirements
description: Build an initial Habeas requirement set from an existing codebase by tracing its tests and user-visible behavior; use for requirements bootstrapping or coverage audits.
# Bootstrap requirements

Read the project's existing requirements, documentation, public entry points, implementation, and tests before writing new requirements. Follow behavior through the code rather than relying only on test names or top-level dispatch.
Keep two working inventories:
- Every first-party runnable test or test case, including integration tests, doctests, and parameterized cases where present. Record the requirement or example IDs each test checks.

- Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources, including trait declarations, test helpers, and internal helpers. Record its file location and the requirement or example IDs it cites. Also inventory relevant public APIs, commands, handlers, UI actions, configuration, outputs, errors, and distinct observable branches. Do not count one tagged entry point as coverage for deeper code.
Exclude generated and third-party code from the inventories. If a candidate looks user-facing but its purpose is unclear, keep it on the gap list until resolved.

Treat requirements inferred from existing code as proposals. Show the user their proposed full IDs and exact text, along with uncertainty about whether observed behavior is intended or a bug. Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook; prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.

Create or reuse the agreed, stable, chapter-qualified `{req}` requirements in the mdBook. State observable obligations with BCP 14 terms. Group tests that check the same behavior under one requirement; several tests MAY share an ID. For tests of internal invariants, write a requirement for the invariant they actually check rather than inventing a user-facing promise. Distinguish intended behavior from a possible bug or incidental implementation detail.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. An example must cite a requirement, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail`, get the user's agreement, and cite it. Record evidence explaining why each such function adds no end-user-observable behavior beyond the requirements it supports. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Create a function attestation for each such function in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Its purpose is to confirm that the function cites every applicable requirement or named example. Read the entire function and the relevant definitions, including ones not already cited. Explain how you found the relevant set, why the requirements input globs cover it, and how cited texts together account for each observable branch. Add a Rust-item input selecting the function and a requirements input covering every citation. A matching snapshot and citation list are insufficient for a true determination. Reassess after either input changes.

Review every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Verify that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and does not introduce additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite all of them at meaningful implementation points and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. For example, a `^C` shortcut needs a requirement that explains why it is accepted. A tag alone does not establish that the behavior matches the requirement. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and evidence records. Each evidence record must cite exact current lines covering every reference to its definition. Judge each requirement or example from the code and test results; a tag alone does not justify `determination: true`.

For each requirement, assess whether the cited implementation meets its text and whether tests cover the interesting cases. If there are no tests, assess whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence, and explain that judgment. For each example, assess whether tests cover its scenario and expected outcomes; a true judgment requires a covered `{test}` reference and an explanation of the setup and assertions. Use the evidence skill's three outcomes: true for a supported subject, false for unacknowledged gaps or insufficient information, and `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}` for gaps explicitly acknowledged in source comments or tests. Capture the gap descriptions and their issue references or other identifying content in the inputs; references may occur in `FIXME(...)` or elsewhere. Explain their source locations in the rationale. A FIXME does not excuse additional unacknowledged gaps. Function-attestation determinations remain boolean judgments of citation completeness.
For example, source comments can carry these references:
```text
// {test}`requirements.foo`
// {impl}`requirements.foo`

Run the project tests and Habeas validation, then review both inventories independently: Habeas can report an uncited Rust function but cannot judge whether its cited requirements fully explain its behavior. Report test-tag coverage and function coverage as mapped counts over total counts. Claim 100% only when both inventories have no unmapped items and every observable branch has been reviewed. List remaining gaps with file locations and reasons; do not invent evidence or silently exclude difficult cases.
name: habeas-evidence
description: Record and repair Habeas evidence for requirements, examples, source references, and Cargo validation failures.
# Habeas evidence

Run `habeas status [<glob>]` to find requirements and named examples whose evidence needs attention, or add `--all` to see every matching definition. Run `habeas info <glob>` to read definitions, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. Globs match whole names; `*` matches any number of characters, including dots.

For each requirement or example, maintain `evidence/<full-name>.json` with exactly `determination`, `rationale`, `inputs`, and a text field matching the directive: `requirement` for `{req}` or `example` for `{example}`. Copy the current Markdown between the directive's opening and closing fences into that text field, excluding leading and trailing whitespace. Assess the named subject using its cited requirements and definitions as context. Record one of three determinations:
- `true`: the implementation and tests support the whole subject under the review criteria below.

- `false`: an unacknowledged implementation or testing gap remains, or the available information does not support a judgment. Explain the difference between observed noncompliance and missing information in the rationale.

- `{"FIXME": ["#125", "rust-lang/rust#123"]}`: source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, with no additional unacknowledged gap. The array contains at least one nonempty string identifying those gaps by issue reference or other source content. The convention is `FIXME(#125)` or `FIXME(rust-lang/rust#123)`, but references may also appear elsewhere in the inputs. Do not require that exact spelling or invent an issue number. Explain each gap and its source location in the rationale, and capture the comments or tests and any referenced source content as evidence inputs.

CI accepts true and FIXME judgments for requirements and examples when all other evidence checks pass. FIXME remains visible in status and the book; it does not excuse missing, stale, malformed, or uncovered evidence. Function attestations still require true.

An approved requirement or example may be installed before its implementation exists. Record it with `determination: false` and a rationale describing the pending work; an empty `inputs` array is valid until there are lines to cite. Expect validation to fail during this interval. Once code and tests satisfy the approved definition, inspect them, snapshot their exact lines, and only then change the determination to `true`. Review a substantive change to an approved obligation with the user before changing its requirement text.
Each input has one of four forms (the definition form is described below):
- File range: `file`, 1-based inclusive `line_start` and `line_end`, and `text` containing the exact raw lines.
- Rust item: repository-relative `rust_file`, syntactic `rust_item` selector, and `text` containing the complete raw lines, including attached comments, doc comments, and attributes.

- Requirements: `requirements` glob, sorted `matches` of full requirement and named example names, and `text` containing the matched raw fenced declarations in that order, with one blank line between them.
Use `habeas add-input` to capture or refresh an input:
```sh
habeas add-input --for-requirement requirements.ci.inputs --file-range src/evidence.rs:1-20
habeas add-input --for-example reference.cli.unknown_command --rust-item tests/cli.rs:26
habeas add-input --for-rust-item src/evidence.rs 'fn[validate_repository]' --requirements 'requirements.ci.*'

The `--rust-item` input mode selects every Rust item declared on the given line. A named item is declared where its name appears; an unnamed item is declared where its keyword appears. The target flag `--for-rust-item` takes a source path and a selector. An unchanged selector is left untouched; adding or refreshing an input sets the determination to false for review. Every `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference to a definition must fall within one of that definition's resolved input ranges.

For every first-party Rust function or method, maintain exactly one entry in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. The file contains `rust_file` and a `functions` array. Each entry contains `rust_item`, `citations` as objects with `role` and `name`, `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. Give it one Rust-item input selecting its function and at least one requirements input whose matches include all its citations. The attestation confirms that the function carries citations for **every applicable** requirement or named example. Inspect the whole function, search the relevant definitions, and explain how you identified the applicable set, why the input globs cover it, and how the cited texts jointly account for its behavior. A matching snapshot and citation list alone do not justify `determination: true`. Reassess after the function or selected definitions change.
Function-attestation determinations remain boolean and judge citation completeness, not whether the requirements are satisfied.

For a requirement, assess whether the cited code implements it as stated and whether its tests cover the interesting cases in the design space. In the rationale, explain the implementation and testing support. If there are no tests, judge whether the logic is simple enough not to need them or testing is impractical, and explain why. This exception applies to requirements, not examples.

For an example, assess whether tests cover its described scenario and expected outcomes. A true determination requires at least one relevant `{test}` reference covered by an evidence input. In the rationale, name the tests and explain how their setup and assertions cover every interesting aspect and expected result. Inspect the tests and their results; a reference alone does not establish adequate coverage. Use FIXME for explicitly documented coverage gaps under the criteria above, and false for other missing coverage.

When assessing one subject, inspect every end-user-observable result and branch relevant to it, including errors and input handling. Use related requirements as context without making separate judgments about their complete implementation. In a broader code review, confirm that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not prove the behavior is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. Do not waive an uncited function because it is an internal helper. If no behavior-specific requirement explains it, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement, cite it, and give evidence for each such function explaining why it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior. Do not use internal-detail to justify unspecified observable behavior.

Run `cargo test --workspace` after changing requirements, examples, source references, or evidence. Read the full set of Habeas errors: missing and orphan records, malformed fields, false determinations, stale definition text, changed input lines, unknown references, uncovered reference lines, uncited Rust functions, and stale or missing function attestations.
Do not make a failing check green by inventing input text or changing a determination without examining the cited files.
Named definitions use a fourth input form: `definition` (one full definition name)
and `text` (the complete raw fenced declaration, including `:phrase:`). They have
no standalone determination. `habeas add-input` automatically captures definitions
referenced with `{term}` by the subject text or reviewed inputs, including transitive
dependencies. Cycles are allowed; retain one input per definition. Changes to a
phrase or body require reassessment. Requirements globs select requirements and
examples, while their term dependencies are captured separately.

description: Design and vet requirements and examples for user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; maintain definitions and references.
# Habeas requirements
## New or changed behavior

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Run `habeas info <glob>` to read current requirement and named example texts, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. A full name selects exactly; `*` matches any number of characters, including dots, when you need to inspect a group.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior, add tests and traceability references, and maintain evidence. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Use the evidence skill for pending determinations while implementation is incomplete.
## Reviewing code against requirements

For a requirement, assess whether the cited code implements it as stated and whether tests cover the interesting cases in its design space. If there are no tests, assess whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence, and explain that judgment. For an example, assess whether tests cover its scenario and expected outcomes; identify their setup and assertions in the rationale. Keep the assessment focused on the named subject, using referenced requirements and definitions as context.

Requirement and example judgments have three outcomes: `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`. Use FIXME when source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, and record their issue references or other identifying content. A documented gap does not excuse other, unacknowledged gaps. Use the `habeas-evidence` skill for the complete outcome and source-recording guidance.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement, cite it on the function, and record evidence explaining why each such function adds no end-user-observable behavior beyond the requirements it supports. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

Every function also needs an attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Its purpose is to confirm, after reviewing the function and applicable requirement and example texts, that the function carries **all applicable citations**. Search beyond the citations already present, explain how the relevant definitions were identified and why the requirements input globs cover them, and explain how cited texts jointly account for each observable branch. Include one Rust-item input for the function and at least one requirements input covering all cited names. Reassess and set the determination true only after a changed function or selected definition set has been reviewed. The `habeas-evidence` skill gives the authoring commands and schema.
Function-attestation determinations remain boolean and judge citation completeness, not whether the requirements are satisfied.
## Authoring format

Put requirements in the book's Markdown source directory. Define each with a fenced `{req}` directive: the opening line is three or more colons followed by `{req} name`, and the closing line has at least as many colons. Derive the full name from the chapter path relative to that directory: remove `.md`, change `/` to `.`, and append the directive name. For nested chapters, omit a leading `reqs/` and a trailing `/index` or `/README`.
```text
:::{req} forwarding.quit
Pressing q MUST stop managed forwards.

Everything between the fences is the requirement body, including headings and diagrams. Use a longer outer colon fence when the body contains a nested colon directive. Use BCP 14 terms when stating obligations.

Write a concrete case as a separate `{example}` directive with the same chapter-qualified naming and fence rules. Cite at least one requirement it illustrates from the example body. A true example determination needs test references and an evidence rationale explaining how the tests cover its interesting aspects. Keep names unique across requirements and examples.
Use fully qualified names for implementation, citation, and test references. Place them on the relevant source or book line:
```text
{impl}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{cite}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{test}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
When a requirement or example changes, update its `evidence/<full-name>.json` record. Run the Cargo tests to see all Habeas validation findings.
## Shared vocabulary
Use `:::{definition} name` with one nonempty `:phrase: display text` option before
its explanatory body to define shared vocabulary. Reference its chapter-qualified
name with the `{term}` role; the book renders the phrase as a plain link, without
a badge. Names are unique across requirements, examples, and definitions. A
named definition has no evidence record of its own and cannot substitute for a
requirement citation. Dependent evidence snapshots its complete declaration;
review changes to phrases and bodies because they invalidate that evidence.

Each Rust function also needs an attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`, with a `rust_file` field and a `functions` array. Every entry has `rust_item`, a `citations` array of `{ "role": "impl", "name": "requirements.some_name" }` objects, a boolean `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. This determination assesses citation coverage; FIXME applies to requirement and example judgments. It needs one Rust-item input for that function and at least one requirements input covering every cited definition. The agent must review the whole function and relevant definitions, then explain why its citations include *every applicable* requirement or named example and how those texts account for its behavior together.
